must_allow.text: Creatinine is a waste product from muscle activity, and the kidneys normally clear it from the blood.
eGFR is an estimate of how much blood the kidneys filter each minute, calculated from creatinine, age and sex.
HbA1c reflects average blood sugar over roughly the past two to three months, because sugar attaches to hemoglobin in red blood cells.
A fasting glucose test asks you not to eat for about 8 hours so that a recent meal does not raise the reading.
A reference range is the span of values seen in most healthy people tested by that lab; it is a comparison point, not a pass or fail line.
Different labs use different equipment, so their reference ranges can differ slightly for the same test.
LDL cholesterol is sometimes called 'bad' cholesterol because it can build up in artery walls.
HDL cholesterol helps carry other cholesterol back to the liver, which is why higher values are generally seen as protective.
Triglycerides are a type of fat in the blood; levels rise after eating, so this test is often done fasting.
TSH is a signal from the pituitary gland that tells the thyroid how much hormone to make.
Free T4 measures the thyroid hormone that is not bound to proteins and is available to the body.
Ferritin is a protein that stores iron, and its level is used as an indirect measure of the body's iron stores.
Hemoglobin is the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen; it is usually reported in g/dL.
Glucose in the United States is reported in mg/dL, while many other countries use mmol/L; 90 mg/dL is about 5.0 mmol/L.
ALT and AST are enzymes found mainly in liver cells; they are released into the blood when liver cells are stressed.
A complete blood count measures red cells, white cells and platelets in one sample.
Potassium is measured in mmol/L and is kept within a narrow range by the kidneys.
A urinalysis checks the colour, concentration and content of a urine sample, often with a dipstick first.
An INR test measures how long blood takes to clot and is used to monitor warfarin treatment.
Vitamin D is usually measured as 25-hydroxyvitamin D, reported in ng/mL or nmol/L.
Blood pressure has two numbers: systolic, when the heart contracts, and diastolic, between beats.
Lab values are flagged H or L when they fall outside the reference range printed next to them.
Hydration, exercise and the time of day can all shift a lab value a little between tests.
Uric acid is a waste product from breaking down purines, which are found in some foods and in the body's own cells.
A lipid panel is a group of tests done on one blood sample: total cholesterol, LDL, HDL and triglycerides.
High TSH can be seen in people with an underactive thyroid, but it can also be affected by illness, certain medicines and the time of the blood draw.
Low ferritin is one of several findings that clinicians consider when assessing iron deficiency.
Elevated ALT may be associated with fatty liver, alcohol, some medications or a viral infection, among other causes.
An eGFR below 60 on two tests at least three months apart is one criterion clinicians use when evaluating chronic kidney disease.
In general, an HbA1c of 6.5% or higher is one of the thresholds used in the diagnosis of diabetes, together with other tests and a clinical assessment.
Raised CRP is a non-specific sign of inflammation and can be seen with infections, injuries and many long-term conditions.
High uric acid is more common in people who develop gout, though many people with a high value never have symptoms.
Low hemoglobin is sometimes related to iron, vitamin B12 or folate levels, and sometimes to other causes entirely.
Very high triglycerides are, at a population level, associated with a higher risk of pancreatitis.
Elevated potassium can be related to kidney function, some blood pressure medicines, or simply how the sample was handled.
A high white blood cell count may be seen with infection, stress, inflammation or smoking.
LDL levels tend to be higher in families with inherited cholesterol conditions, but diet and other factors also play a large role.
Low vitamin D is common in people who get little sun exposure, especially in winter months.
Protein in the urine is one of the markers clinicians watch in people with diabetes or high blood pressure.
A low MCV is often seen alongside iron deficiency, and less commonly with inherited red cell conditions.
Elevated fasting glucose may reflect prediabetes, diabetes, recent illness, or not having fasted long enough.
Blood pressure readings at or above 130/80 are classed as elevated under some guidelines and as normal under others.
Mild changes in liver enzymes are frequently temporary and can follow a viral illness or a new medication.
Low sodium can be seen in people who drink large amounts of fluid, in some medication users, and in several medical conditions.
High PSA values are not specific; they can be related to prostate enlargement, infection or recent activity as well as cancer.
In population studies, higher HDL cholesterol has been associated with lower cardiovascular risk.
A low platelet count can accompany viral infections, certain medicines and some liver conditions.
Hypothyroidism is one possible reason for a high TSH, and a repeat test is commonly used to see whether the result persists.
An elevated B12 level is uncommon and is more often linked to supplements than to disease.
Among people with type 2 diabetes, kidney function is typically checked at least once a year.
